opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things I find most interesting from the interpretability work we've been doing. At the very start of the model, the token embeddings are pretty language-specific, almost by necessity. The token for "small" in English and "petit" in French are different entries in the vocabulary, so in the earliest layers you see features that are tied to the particular language and even the particular spelling or tokenization.

What we see as you move into the middle of the model is that those representations start to converge. When we trace what the model is doing on something like "the opposite of small is," the features doing the real conceptual work, like a notion of "smallness," a notion of "antonym," and then "largeness," are largely shared across English, French, Chinese, and so on. Language-specific machinery sits at the edges. Early on, there are features that read in the particular language and map it into this more abstract space. Near the end, there are features that take the abstract answer and say, "okay, we're writing in French, so output 'grand.'"

So the way I think about it is that the initial embeddings are a kind of input adapter. They have to be specific because the vocabulary is specific. But the model seems to learn fairly quickly that it's much more efficient to share the computation in the middle than to learn separate circuits for every language. We also saw that the fraction of shared features tends to grow with model scale, so bigger models seem to be more language-agnostic in that middle region.

That has a nice practical implication. It helps explain why something you learn in one language can transfer to another. If a fact or a skill lives in this shared conceptual space, then you don't have to relearn it from scratch for each language. You just need the input and output layers to connect to it.

r001.rationale: It says representations converge in the middle layers, where conceptual features are shared across English, French, Chinese, and other languages.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes language-specific early features tied to vocabulary and tokenization from shared semantic features such as smallness and antonymy.

r003.rationale: It says antonym-related features are shared across languages, but does not state that the same intervention on that representation works across languages.

r004.rationale: It describes facts and skills transferring between languages, but does not state that a circuit learned from text in one language can be applied while processing text in another.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a fair amount of time on, and I think the cleanest way to say it is that the token embeddings are kind of the raw material, and the shared representations are what the model builds out of that raw material a few layers in.

So when you look at the very first layer, the embedding is really just a lookup. The token for "small" in English and the token for "petit" in French are completely different entries in that table, and if you look at them, they don't have much to do with each other. They're language-specific, they're surface-level, they encode things like "this is a piece of a word, here's roughly what kind of word it is." There's not a lot of meaning there yet.

And then what we found, especially as you go to larger models, is that pretty quickly the model collapses those into something that looks much more abstract. If you ask Claude for the opposite of "small" in English, French, and Chinese, you see the same features light up in the middle of the network. There's a feature for the concept of smallness, there's a feature for "antonym" or "opposite of," and those are shared regardless of what language the prompt came in. The language itself gets sort of factored out and tracked separately, and then it gets reintroduced at the end when the model has to decide which actual token to emit.

So the relationship is really this funnel. You start with embeddings that are tied to specific strings in specific languages, the model maps many of them onto a shared conceptual space, does its reasoning there, and then maps back out. And one thing that was striking is how much more of that sharing there is in bigger models. In the small models, there's a lot more per-language machinery. In the larger ones, a much bigger fraction of the features are genuinely multilingual.

I think that also tells you something about what the embeddings are and aren't. People sometimes want to read a lot into the embedding geometry, and you can find some structure there, but most of the interesting stuff isn't in the embedding. It's in what the model does with it in the first few layers, and that's where the cross-lingual story actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response says that language-specific embeddings are mapped, as processing proceeds, into a shared conceptual space.

r002.rationale: It describes shared semantic features such as smallness and opposition, while language is tracked separately and later reintroduced; this indicates selected facets are shared rather than every embedding aspect.

r003.rationale: It reports that the same features activate for an opposite-word task across languages, but does not say that the same intervention on the shared representation works across languages.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that a circuit learned from text in one language can be applied while processing another.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to distinguish the initial token embeddings from the representations the model builds as it processes a sentence. At the input, each token has a learned vector, and that vector doesn’t depend on the context. So two words with similar meanings in different languages can start with quite different embeddings.

But those embeddings are just the starting point. As you go through the layers, the model combines information from the surrounding tokens and builds contextual representations. Because the same model is learning across languages, it can develop features that are useful across those languages—features that capture something about meaning or grammatical relationships, for example.

That doesn’t necessarily mean there’s a single, perfectly language-independent representation somewhere in the model. You can have shared features alongside language-specific information. So I wouldn’t look at the initial embeddings alone to judge how much the model shares across languages. A lot of that sharing can emerge in the computation that happens afterward.

r001.rationale: It says processing can develop features useful across languages that capture meaning, and that sharing can emerge in later computation.

r002.rationale: It describes shared features alongside language-specific information, rather than claiming all aspects of the initial embeddings are shared.

r003.rationale: It does not mention an intervention on shared representations of opposition or say that one works across languages.

r004.rationale: It does not describe applying a circuit learned from one language to text in another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate the initial token embeddings from the representations the model builds as it processes a sentence. The initial embedding is associated with a token, so two words with similar meanings in different languages can start with quite different vectors. There’s no requirement that they be close together.

But those embeddings are just the starting point. As the model moves through its layers, it builds contextual representations. Training on multiple languages can encourage it to reuse some of the same features for similar concepts or relationships across languages, because that helps it predict text.

So shared representations don’t necessarily mean there’s a single universal embedding for each concept. They can emerge deeper in the network, and they can be partially shared while still preserving information about the language and the particular way something was expressed.

r001.rationale: It says multilingual training can lead the model to reuse features for similar concepts across languages as it builds contextual representations through its layers.

r002.rationale: It describes representations as partially shared while retaining language and expression information, rather than sharing every aspect of the initial embeddings.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss an intervention on a shared representation of opposition or its effect across languages.

r004.rationale: It does not state that a circuit learned from one language can be applied to another.
